tests.weakness: Secret-bearing pages (config backups, .env, decommissioned admin notes) are indexable; robots.txt advertises them. An in-range crawler/search index stands in for a public engine.
tests.degraded: In-range search index replaces a public search engine; the lab performs no outbound queries. Dorking syntax (site:/inurl:/intitle:) and the leaked-content outcome are faithful.

tests.weakness: server_tokens on (nginx) and ServerTokens Full (Apache) disclose exact versions in headers and error pages.
Metafiles enumerate hidden paths, allow any RIA cross-domain access, and leak internal hosts and a stale security contact.
Nine published ports across proxy, cache, admin, DNS, S3 and an unauthenticated datastore, plus a sitemap enumerating unlinked paths.
HTML comments carry DB credentials and internal IPs; hidden fields carry a tenant id; inline JS hardcodes a live API key.
GET and POST entry points with reflected parameters, hidden fields, and header/cookie-driven behaviour are all discoverable from the homepage.
A three-hop link chain reaches a data-export endpoint that is never linked from the homepage, so only path mapping finds it.
Werkzeug/Flask error pages disclose the framework and its exact version.
Application name, version and build number are disclosed in a meta generator tag, a response header and a public changelog.
Proxy, cache, application and database tiers each identify themselves through headers and responses, allowing the full architecture to be mapped from outside.
An unauthenticated Redis instance is published to the host, and backend infrastructure services are reachable from the edge network.
Default 'It works!' page, vendor sample content and platform-wide directory listing left enabled.
Sensitive extensions are served as text/plain; PHP source is disclosed because no handler is configured.
A real tarball backup containing .env and secrets, editor swap files, .DS_Store and a decommissioned admin directory with credentials are all retrievable.
Adminer, Apache server-status/server-info and nginx stub_status are exposed without authentication; the app admin login accepts default credentials.
TraceEnable On echoes requests; anonymous WebDAV allows PUT/DELETE/MKCOL on both nginx and Apache.
HTTPS is served without Strict-Transport-Security, and HTTP serves the application instead of redirecting to TLS.
Upload directory is 0777 (world-writable), secret config is 0644 (world-readable), and the web root is writable by the anonymous WebDAV user.
A deprovisioned SaaS site left a live CNAME. The provider returns the characteristic unclaimed-host 404 and lets anyone claim the hostname, completing a real takeover.
An S3 bucket carries a public-read ACL and an Allow Principal:* policy, and anonymous callers can read customer PII and a portal .env from it. A sibling bucket is correctly marked private.
tests.degraded: LocalStack's S3 does not enforce authorization for anonymous requests, so the private sibling bucket cannot be shown returning 403. Bucket ACL/policy inspection and the anonymous public exposure of PII are faithful; the enforcement contrast is not.

tests.weakness: CSP uses 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval' and wildcard sources; other pages send no CSP at all.
nginx alias traversal escapes the static root; a slash-less proxy prefix lets /apiadmin/users bypass the deny rule on /admin; merge_slashes off adds a further normalisation gap.
X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy and the Cross-Origin-* policies are all absent.
The full feature-flag inventory is public and a privileged console is gated on a client-controlled cookie/header rather than the user's role.
Varnish keys the cache on URL only while the backend reflects X-Forwarded-Host into a cacheable response, so one poisoned request is served to all later visitors.
